title: Wildfires, Preparedness and the Two Departments
label: 15 September 2026 · Wildfire evidence
summary: Two ministers and two officials told the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee that this summer's record wildfire season has exposed gaps in co-ordination, resources, aerial firefighting and rebuilding, but they disagreed with MPs over land management, controlled burning, and how quickly real change will arrive. The witnesses accepted that current arrangements are not fit for the future, promised a faster and better-prepared approach before next spring, and pointed to a Prime Ministerial wildfire summit in October as the moment when evidence will be pulled together.

chapters.title: A Summer That Changed Things
chapters.takeaway: Ministers admitted this summer's record fires have exposed that current arrangements are not fit for future risk.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This summer brought record wildfires, and 19 homes were destroyed with over 50,000 acres burned. Ministers, what lessons has the Government drawn?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We're in a very different place coming out of this summer than going in. The hottest summer on record may be the coolest we'll ever have. Over 1,300 fires. What we have now won't be fit for managing fires in 10 years' time.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The fire service response was extraordinary. The real step change is the impact on urban fringes. This wasn't just rural moorland; it threatened homes and infrastructure. We need prevention, mitigation and recovery, not just response.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Rural communities have lived with this for years. The fires were ablaze for weeks, but only after they hit the suburbs did the Prime Minister convene Cobra. From 22 July to 14 August we had no fire minister at all. What does that say about priority?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Timing is everything. There was a change of administration. But the Prime Minister is committed to a wildfire summit in October, bringing together everyone involved, including community voices.

chapters.title: Who Is In Charge?
chapters.takeaway: MPs pressed the two Departments on co-ordination, borders and whether there is a single person in charge.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is this now a national issue needing a more co-ordinated UK-wide approach?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The situation in south Wales shows we must work across borders, respecting devolution but sharing resources. I haven't yet spoken to my opposite numbers in the devolved administrations.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Why are we having a national summit but a disjointed approach with Wales? Has MHCLG reached out?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We engage regularly with counterparts in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. I've never had any rebuff. My team was in Scotland three weeks ago talking to their fire service and government.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A ministerial lead makes these things more effective. That's something to take away.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Fires don't respect borders, so we need a joined-up approach. But we're not going to fight fires from Whitehall alone. We need investment on the ground with MHCLG, landowners and land managers.

chapters.title: Aerial Firefighting and Deadlines
chapters.takeaway: The UK lacks a dedicated aerial firefighting capability, and officials admitted there are no firm deadlines yet, only a promise to be better by next summer.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: We don't have a dedicated aerial firefighting capability; we rely on local commercial arrangements. Is that sufficient?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: This is top of the agenda for the summit. Fire chiefs say aerial support is good at putting out flames but less good at dealing with deep-seated fire. It's absolutely a priority.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We did have some national assets, but not aerial ones like other countries. Individual fire services looking for commercial arrangements mid-response isn't going to cut it. We're looking at cost-effective on-call availability. 44 services competing for the same asset isn't efficient.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We're also looking at drones, surveillance and water-carrying technology. We need to solve it for next summer and look to the future.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you have a timeline?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We want to be in a much better place by next summer. We're talking to providers now. What I want to hold myself accountable for is that by next summer we're in a much better place than we were this summer.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You start conversations, procurement happens, you liaise with devolved administrations. You're telling me you haven't set deadlines.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: The wildfire season can start in spring, or earlier. That's when I want this in place. There are complexities.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about military assets? We saw Chinooks in Cyprus. Have you considered using retiring RAF Chinooks?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: The RAF is involved in discussions. Nothing is off the table, military, public agencies or private sector. I can't go into the detail on the Chinooks.

chapters.title: Land Management and Burning
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA and MPs clashed over controlled burning, with officials insisting rewetting and licensing are the right approach and MPs accusing them of ignoring ground evidence.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Why does England still not have a national wildfire strategy? Will one be published before next season?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We have an action plan leading into the summit. I think of it as one, two and 10-year vision. I want us in a stronger place by spring next year. This is iterative. We'll gather evidence and make it public.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The National Fire Chiefs Council says water availability is a growing challenge. Are you considering stronger requirements on water companies?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I don't have a specific answer on that. We're gathering evidence. Water companies are represented on local resilience forums. We'll take that away.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Water companies have a legal duty to maintain emergency preparedness. Fire services have alternatives, tactical burning, high-volume pumps, seawater. But yes, it's important they have the water they need.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On controlled burning, there were 24 licence applications and only two approved. Is that not evidence the 2025 regulations are too restrictive?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: We haven't had many credible applications. Most were for training, and the fire service advises training elsewhere. If a credible application comes in, we'll issue it. We're in live conversations with the CLA about making the process more flexible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Secretary of State said there's no place for this. Are you determined to leave fire load on the hill?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: We're not determined to leave fire load. But if the long-term aim is rewetting, cool burning messes with hydrology. We want to move to wetter peatland. There's a transition.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You're making decisions on an evidence review that didn't even look at wildfire risk. Does that not concern you?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: When ministers made the regulations, they consulted widely, including the National Fire Chiefs Council. We take fire service advice on every licence application. You never have a perfect evidence base.

chapters.title: Alerts, Risk and Planning
chapters.takeaway: The emergency alert worked but had teething problems, the national risk register understates wildfire risk and will be updated, and planning rules are starting to reflect fire risk.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should the emergency alert have been issued sooner?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: It was decided at Cobra. On balance it was welcomed. But there are issues around vulnerable people and the Welsh/English sequencing. We'll learn from it and use it judiciously to avoid complacency.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The decision was taken on the advice of the fire and rescue service, not politicians. Some people got six alerts because of poor signal. That's feeding into the lessons learned. Overall it was important and successful in raising awareness.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: All alerts are technically issued by the Cabinet Office. The decision-making body is normally Cobra.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The national risk register still calls the reasonable worst-case wildfire scenario remote, around 1%, less likely than an earthquake. Is that accurate?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: You're right. The speed of change this summer was significant. We need to review the risk assessment. The worst case is more than one major wildfire happening, and we saw multiple major incidents at once. Wildfires are now more likely than earthquakes. We'll start that conversation with the Cabinet Office and update it before next season.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On planning, what role did fire services have in the 2026 national planning policy framework and its wildfire risk reference?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: I wasn't directly involved. I believe fire was involved via the National Fire Chiefs Council. I can provide details subsequently.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about simple planning mitigations, fire breaks, tracks, water storage on farms?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Absolutely. Water resilience and wildfire go hand in hand. We want to drive forward water capture on farmland, and changes were announced in the last NPPF round on reservoirs.

chapters.title: Farms, Water and Communities
chapters.takeaway: Farmers and landowners are vital first responders, but water supply, funding and the emotional toll remain unresolved.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Water availability is a challenge. The New Forest fire had supply problems. What responsibility should water companies have?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We need water resilience. The Government worked with water companies on temporary use bans this summer. Water companies must invest in infrastructure and provide resilience.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Farmers are on the frontline. Will you tackle planning and abstraction barriers for on-farm reservoirs, and will there be more funding windows?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The £15 million comes with a commitment to unlock barriers. We're working with MHCLG on planning. Write in to the Department, Minister Hardy leads on water. There's good local work in Dorset with farmers and fire services.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're working with the NFU on an evidence-led review around permitted development rights for on-farm reservoirs. We want to give farmers more control over water storage.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about the emotional and physical toll on firefighters and communities? And should farmers get monetary recognition for their response?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're looking carefully at the health and wellbeing needs of firefighters. It's critical we look after the people who keep us safe. Resilience and prevention will become more important as these events continue.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Farmers played a critical role. We need to make sure they're accessing the schemes and grants available, because uptake is currently not full.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On adaptation, the Climate Change Committee called NAP3 not fit for purpose. Do you share that assessment?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: That's before my time. We're in a very different place now. We'll respond to the fourth risk assessment in January 2027 and set bolder objectives in NAP4. But we won't wait until 2028 for everything.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Why should homeowners be confident you'll be better prepared next season?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I've asked officials to look at one, two and 10-year goals. We must be in a better place by spring. There are measures we can take this winter, water storage, access to ELM schemes. Flooding was once unmanaged; we've come a long way. We need that blueprint for wildfire.
